questions.question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from USSR (Now Russia)?

options.text: Residuary powers vest with the centre
Centre appoints the Governors at the states

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fundamental Duties**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The concept of **Fundamental Duties** in the Indian Constitution is inspired by the Constitution of the **USSR (now Russia)**.
 
• These duties were added to the Indian Constitution through the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** during the tenure of Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**.
 
• The Fundamental Duties are enshrined under **Part IVA** of the Indian Constitution in **Article 51A**.
 
• Originally, there were **10 Fundamental Duties**, but later one more was added by the **86th Amendment Act, 2002**, bringing the total to **11 duties**.
 
• The Fundamental Duties primarily aim to promote a sense of **patriotism** and to uphold the **unity and integrity** of the nation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Features of Fundamental Duties:**

 
 
• These duties are **non-justiciable**, meaning they cannot be enforced by the courts.
 
• They act as a constant reminder to citizens about their responsibilities towards the nation.
 
• The Fundamental Duties emphasize respecting the **Constitution, the national flag, and the national anthem**.
 
• They aim to promote **scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform**.
 
 
 
• **Other Features Borrowed from Different Countries:**
 
 
• **Residuary powers vest with the centre** – This feature is borrowed from the **Canadian Constitution**.
 
• **The Preamble of the Constitution** – The idea of a preamble is inspired by the **United States Constitution**.
 
• **Centre appoints the Governors at the states** – This is a feature influenced by the **Government of India Act, 1935**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Fundamental Duties:**
 
 
• They serve as a moral compass and guide citizens in their **conduct and behavior**.
 
• They ensure that citizens uphold the **sovereignty, unity, and integrity** of India.
 
• They aim to create a sense of **responsibility** and **civic consciousness** among citizens.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties in Practice:**
 
 
• Citizens are expected to protect the **environment** and safeguard public property.
 
• They are also encouraged to promote **harmony** and work towards the **eradication of practices derogatory to the dignity of women**.
 
• While not legally enforceable, these duties play a crucial role in shaping responsible citizens.

questions.question: Which of the following country is NOT the founding member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iraq**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO)** is a Eurasian political, economic, and security alliance established on **15 June 2001** in **Shanghai, China**.
 
• The founding members of SCO are **China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan**.
 
• **Iraq** is not a member of the SCO, neither as a founding member nor as a subsequent member. It is located in the Middle East and has no direct involvement with the Eurasian-focused organization.
 
• The primary goals of the SCO include promoting **mutual trust, cooperation, regional stability, and countering terrorism**, extremism, and separatism among its member states.
 
• In 2017, the SCO expanded its membership to include **India and Pakistan**, making the organization more diverse and influential.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO):**

 
 
• The SCO was initially formed as the **Shanghai Five** in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan to resolve border disputes and promote regional security.
 
• Uzbekistan joined the group in 2001, and it was officially renamed the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.
 
• The headquarters of the SCO is located in **Beijing, China**.
 
 
 
• **Key Functions of SCO:**
 
 
• Focuses on **counter-terrorism**, combating drug trafficking, and fostering economic, cultural, and humanitarian cooperation among its members.
 
• It established the **Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS)** in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, to coordinate counter-terrorism efforts.
 
 
 
• **Membership Expansion:**
 
 
• **India** and **Pakistan** became full members in **2017**, marking a significant expansion in the organization's scope and influence.
 
• The inclusion of these South Asian nations added to the SCO's strategic depth and economic potential.
 
 
 
• **Iraq:**
 
 
• **Iraq** is located in the Middle East and is a member of the **Arab League, Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC)**, and other international organizations.
 
• Iraq's focus has historically been on its regional and internal affairs rather than participating in Eurasian regional alliances like the SCO.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Strategic Importance of SCO:**

 
 
• The SCO covers approximately **60% of Eurasia** and has a population of over **3 billion people**, making it one of the largest regional organizations in terms of geographical scope and population.
 
• It acts as a counterbalance to Western organizations such as **NATO** and promotes a multipolar world order.
 
 
 
• **SCO Observers and Dialogue Partners:**
 
 
• The SCO also includes observer states and dialogue partners, such as **Iran, Afghanistan, and Belarus**, which aim to enhance their engagement with the organization.
 
• **Iraq** is not part of these categories, further emphasizing its non-affiliation with the SCO.

questions.question: In 2024, women from how many states accounted for 49% of all self-monitoring female borrowers in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **49% of self-monitoring female borrowers** in India in **2024** were concentrated in women from only **3 states**, highlighting the regional disparity in access to financial opportunities for women.
 
• These **3 states** likely contributed significantly due to factors such as **higher microfinance penetration**, established **self-help group (SHG) networks**, and better financial literacy programs targeting women.
 
• The dominance of these states in terms of women's participation in self-monitoring borrowing could also be attributed to **state-specific policies** promoting microfinance and small-scale entrepreneurship.
 
• Other options (5, 8, 11, and more states) are incorrect as they overestimate the number of states contributing to the specified percentage (49%) of self-monitoring female borrowers, based on the available data for 2024.
 
• This statistic underscores the need to expand financial inclusion efforts to other states to ensure equitable participation by women nationwide.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Self-monitoring female borrowers:**

 
 
• Women borrowers who actively monitor their financial activities and repayments are often part of **microfinance institutions (MFIs)** or **self-help groups (SHGs)**.
 
• These systems promote **empowerment**, financial independence, and entrepreneurship among women, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• Self-monitoring ensures better **repayment rates** and encourages disciplined financial behavior.
 
 
 
• **Regional disparity in financial inclusion:**
 
 
• Some states, such as **Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal** (examples), have been early adopters of microfinance initiatives, resulting in higher participation.
 
• Other states may lag due to **lack of infrastructure, financial literacy, or cultural barriers**.
 
• This highlights the need for targeted interventions and support to less-performing states to ensure balanced growth.
 
 
 
• **Role of microfinance and SHGs:**
 
 
• Microfinance and SHGs play a critical role in **alleviating poverty**, especially among women, by providing small loans for entrepreneurship and other income-generating activities.
 
• They also foster **social cohesion** and help women build networks for mutual support and learning.
 
 
 
• **Government initiatives:**
 
 
• Programs like **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** are aimed at promoting financial inclusion and strengthening SHGs.
 
• Other initiatives, such as **Jan Dhan Yojana**, aim to improve access to banking and financial services for marginalized groups, including women.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Microfinance penetration:** States with a higher penetration of microfinance institutions often see greater participation of women in borrowing activities, as these institutions primarily target women borrowers.
 
• **Financial literacy programs:** Effective financial literacy campaigns improve women's confidence in managing loans and participating in formal financial systems.
 
• **Policy support:** State-specific schemes promoting women entrepreneurs and SHGs contribute significantly to financial inclusion.
 
• **Challenges:** Despite progress, many women still face barriers such as **limited access to credit**, cultural restrictions, and lack of awareness about financial products.

questions.question: The PM POSHAN scheme is being implemented by the Ministry of ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Education**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **PM POSHAN Scheme**, previously known as the **Mid-Day Meal Scheme**, is implemented by the **Ministry of Education** in India.
 
• The scheme aims to provide **nutritious meals** to children studying in government and government-aided schools, ensuring their overall development and addressing malnutrition.
 
• It covers **students from Classes 1 to 8** and is designed to support education by improving enrollment, retention, and attendance rates.
 
• The scheme is operational in all states and union territories, benefiting millions of children across the country.
 
• The **Ministry of Education** oversees the planning, funding, implementation, and monitoring of the scheme, with cooperation from state governments and local administrative bodies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **PM POSHAN Scheme Objectives:**

 
 
• To improve **nutritional levels** among school-going children, especially those from economically weaker sections.
 
• To enhance **enrollment, attendance, and retention** rates in primary and upper primary schools.
 
• To promote **social equity** by ensuring all children, regardless of caste, religion, or economic status, receive meals together.
 
 
 
• **Implementation:**
 
 
• The scheme is jointly funded by the **Central and State Governments** under a cost-sharing basis.
 
• Meals are prepared in hygienic conditions and served to children during school hours.
 
• Local community involvement, including **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)** and **non-governmental organizations (NGOs)**, ensures effective implementation.
 
 
 
• **Coverage:**
 
 
• The scheme benefits children studying in government and government-aided schools, **Education Guarantee Scheme (EGS) centers**, and **Alternative and Innovative Education (AIE) centers**.
 
• Approximately **11.8 crore children** in India are beneficiaries of the scheme.
 
 
 
• **Impact:**
 
 
• The scheme has contributed to a reduction in **dropout rates** and an increase in school enrollment, especially among girls and children from disadvantaged groups.
 
• It has helped in addressing the issue of **hidden hunger** and improving the overall health of children.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Background:**

 
 
• The Mid-Day Meal Scheme was first launched in **1995** as a centrally sponsored scheme under the Ministry of Education.
 
• In **2021**, the scheme was renamed as **PM POSHAN (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman)**.
 
 
 
• **Monitoring Mechanism:**
 
 
• The scheme is monitored through regular inspections by **state governments**, **district authorities**, and local-level committees.
 
• Real-time monitoring systems, including the use of technology, have been introduced to track the distribution of meals and ensure transparency.
 
 
 
• **Challenges:**
 
 
• Issues such as **irregular fund flow**, **poor infrastructure**, and **quality control** in meal preparation remain concerns.
 
• The government continues to focus on addressing these challenges through capacity building and policy initiatives.

questions.question: The Chillai Kalan is the local name given to the 40-day period of harsh winter in which of the following region of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jammu and Kashmir**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chillai Kalan** is a term used to describe the **40-day harsh winter period** in the region of **Jammu and Kashmir**, starting from **December 21 to January 31** each year.
 
• During this period, the weather is characterized by **extreme cold**, with temperatures often dropping below **freezing point**, particularly in areas like **Srinagar**.
 
• It is considered the **coldest part of winter**, and snowfall during Chillai Kalan is usually heavy and frequent, significantly impacting daily life and transportation in the region.
 
• The period is crucial for replenishing water resources, as the snow accumulated during Chillai Kalan melts gradually in spring and summer, feeding rivers and streams.
 
• The harsh weather conditions lead to increased use of traditional heating methods like **Kangri** (an earthen pot used by locals to keep warm) and specialized winter clothing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geography of Jammu and Kashmir:**

 
 
• The region is located in the northernmost part of India, surrounded by the **Himalayas**.
 
• It is known for its **cold climate**, especially during winter, and experiences heavy snowfall during Chillai Kalan.
 
• The **Dal Lake** and other water bodies in Srinagar often freeze during this period due to sub-zero temperatures.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Chillai Kalan:**
 
 
• The period plays an important role in maintaining the **hydrological cycle** of the region, as the melting snow ensures adequate water supply during summer.
 
• Local traditions and festivals are influenced by Chillai Kalan, with many families preparing special foods and engaging in cultural activities to cope with the extreme cold.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Daily Life:**
 
 
• Transportation and accessibility are significantly affected due to heavy snowfall, making roads and highways difficult to navigate.
 
• Residents rely on traditional heating systems like the **Kangri** and wear woolen clothing to combat the cold.
 
• Tourists visiting the region during Chillai Kalan often enjoy the scenic beauty of snow-covered landscapes, contributing to **winter tourism**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Regions:**
 
 
• Unlike Jammu and Kashmir, regions like **Himachal Pradesh** and **Arunachal Pradesh** experience cold winters but do not have a defined 40-day period like Chillai Kalan.
 
• **Uttar Pradesh** experiences relatively mild winters compared to Jammu and Kashmir.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Traditional Practices:**

 
 
• Locals use a **Kangri**, a portable heating device, to keep warm during Chillai Kalan.
 
• Special winter foods like **Harissa**, a meat-based dish, are popular during this time to maintain body heat.
 
 
 
• **Tourism:**
 
 
• Chillai Kalan attracts tourists who enjoy activities like **skiing** and exploring the snow-covered landscapes.
 
• Places like **Gulmarg** and **Pahalgam** become hubs for winter sports and sightseeing.

questions.question: The main temple of Shri Jagannath is an impressive and amazing structure constructed in Kalinga architecture, with a height of ____ meters placed on an elevated platform.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**85 meters**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The main temple of **Shri Jagannath** is located in **Puri, Odisha**, and is a part of the famous Char Dham pilgrimage sites in India.
 
• The temple was constructed in the **Kalinga architecture style**, which is characterized by its distinct spire (Shikhara) and intricate carvings on the walls.
 
• The temple stands at an impressive height of **85 meters**, making it one of the tallest Hindu temples in India.
 
• The structure is built on an **elevated platform**, enhancing its grandeur and visibility from a distance.
 
• The temple was originally constructed in the **12th century** by King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kalinga Architecture:**

 
 
• Kalinga architecture is a style of temple architecture that originated in the ancient Kalinga region (modern-day Odisha and parts of Andhra Pradesh).
 
• It is characterized by **Rekha Deula** (tall spire), **Pidha Deula** (pyramidal roof), and **Khakhara Deula** (rectangular structures).
 
• The use of **sandstone** and **laterite** as building materials is a hallmark of this architectural style.
 
 
 
• **Shri Jagannath Temple:**
 
 
• The temple is dedicated to **Lord Jagannath**, a form of Lord Vishnu, along with his siblings **Balabhadra** and **Subhadra**.
 
• The temple is famous for its **annual Rath Yatra** (Chariot Festival), during which the deities are placed on massive chariots and pulled through the streets of Puri.
 
• The temple complex covers an area of approximately **400,000 square feet** and includes several smaller shrines and structures.
 
 
 
• **Important Features of the Temple:**
 
 
• The temple is known for its **Nilachakra**, a sacred wheel made of eight metals, placed atop the spire.
 
• It has four gates: **Simhadwara (Lion Gate)**, **Hastidwara (Elephant Gate)**, **Vyaghradwara (Tiger Gate)**, and **Ashwadwara (Horse Gate)**.
 
• The temple kitchen is considered the **largest kitchen in the world**, preparing food for thousands of devotees daily.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• The Jagannath Temple is an important center of Vaishnavism and has been a site of pilgrimage for centuries.
 
• It was constructed under the patronage of the **Eastern Ganga dynasty**, which ruled Odisha during the medieval period.
 
• The temple is also associated with several legends and myths, such as the story of Lord Jagannath's wooden idols being carved by divine intervention.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tourism and Economy:** The Jagannath Temple is a major tourist attraction and contributes significantly to the economy of Puri and Odisha.
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Site:** The temple has been proposed to be included in the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
 
• **Rath Yatra:** The festival draws millions of devotees and tourists, making it one of the largest religious gatherings in the world.
 
• **Preservation Efforts:** The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is actively involved in the preservation and restoration of the temple.

questions.question: Generally, satellites do not fly below ____ km.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**180 km**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Satellites generally do not fly below 180 km** because of the effects of atmospheric drag. At lower altitudes, the density of Earth's atmosphere increases significantly, creating resistance that slows down the satellite and causes it to lose altitude rapidly.
 
• The minimum altitude for most satellites is usually above **180 km** to ensure stability and longevity of their orbit. Below this, satellites would require constant propulsion to maintain their trajectory.
 
• The region below 180 km is considered part of the upper atmosphere, where air molecules are present in sufficient density to create significant drag forces, making it unsuitable for sustained satellite operation.
 
• Satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) typically operate at altitudes between **180 km and 2,000 km**, providing a balance between proximity to Earth for communication and reduced atmospheric drag.
 
• Flying at altitudes below 180 km would lead to a rapid orbital decay, necessitating frequent re-boosts to maintain altitude, which is not energy efficient.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Atmospheric Drag:**

 
 
• Atmospheric drag is a force exerted by air molecules on satellites as they orbit Earth. It is proportional to the density of the atmosphere.
 
• At altitudes below 180 km, atmospheric drag becomes significant enough to decelerate satellites, causing them to lose altitude and eventually burn up upon re-entry.
 
 
 
• **Low Earth Orbit (LEO):**
 
 
• LEO extends from approximately 180 km to 2,000 km above Earth’s surface.
 
• Satellites in LEO are used for various purposes such as Earth observation, communication, and scientific research.
 
• Examples of satellites in LEO include the **International Space Station (ISS)**, which orbits at an altitude of about 400 km.
 
 
 
• **Orbital Decay:**
 
 
• Orbital decay occurs when a satellite loses energy due to drag, causing it to spiral downward toward Earth.
 
• Sustained operations below 180 km are impractical due to rapid orbital decay.
 
 
 
• **Geostationary and Higher Orbits:**
 
 
• Satellites in geostationary orbits are positioned approximately 35,786 km above Earth, where atmospheric drag is negligible.
 
• These orbits are used for applications such as weather monitoring and telecommunications.
 
 
 
• **Historical Examples:**
 
 
• Early satellites like **Sputnik 1**, launched in 1957, orbited at an altitude of approximately 215 km initially but decayed rapidly due to drag.
 
• Modern satellites are designed to operate at higher altitudes for better efficiency and durability.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Benefits of Higher Altitude Orbits:**

 
 
• Higher altitudes reduce atmospheric drag, enhancing the longevity of satellites.
 
• They provide a wider coverage area, which is advantageous for communication and monitoring purposes.
 
 
 
• **Challenges of Lower Altitudes:**
 
 
• Satellites require more fuel for frequent altitude corrections due to drag at lower altitudes.
 
• Increased risk of re-entry and destruction due to atmospheric friction.

questions.question: The amount of heat energy that is required to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at atmospheric pressure at its melting point is known as the ____ heat of fusion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**latent heat of fusion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Latent heat of fusion** is the amount of heat energy required to change **1 kg of a solid into liquid** at its **melting point** under atmospheric pressure without any change in temperature.
 
• The energy supplied is used to overcome the **forces of attraction between particles** in the solid, allowing it to transition into a liquid state.
 
• This concept is important in understanding phase transitions in substances, such as when **ice melts to water** or metals are melted for industrial applications.
 
• The latent heat of fusion is specific to each substance and is usually measured in **joules per kilogram (J/kg)**.
 
• For example, the latent heat of fusion of **water** is approximately **334,000 J/kg**, meaning it takes this much energy to convert 1 kg of ice at 0°C to water at 0°C.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Phase Transitions:**

 
 
• When a substance transitions between solid, liquid, and gas phases, energy is absorbed or released without changing its temperature.
 
• **Latent heat of vaporization:** The energy required to convert a liquid into a gas without a temperature change.
 
• **Sublimation:** The direct conversion of a solid into a gas, bypassing the liquid phase. This process also involves latent heat.
 
 
 
• **Boiling Point vs. Melting Point:**
 
 
• The **boiling point** is the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas, while the **melting point** is the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
 
• Both processes require energy input, but the type of latent heat involved differs: fusion for melting, vaporization for boiling.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Latent Heat:**
 
 
• Used in **refrigeration and air conditioning systems** to absorb and release heat efficiently.
 
• Plays a critical role in **meteorological phenomena**, such as the formation of clouds and precipitation.
 
• Important in industrial processes like **metal casting** and **welding**, where substances are melted and reshaped.
 
 
 
• **Specific Characteristics of Related Options:**
 
 
• **Boiling:** Refers to the phase transition from liquid to gas, requiring latent heat of vaporization.
 
• **Melting:** Refers to the physical transition from solid to liquid, governed by latent heat of fusion.
 
• **Absolute:** This term is unrelated to phase transitions; it typically refers to numerical values such as absolute temperature.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Measurement Units:** Latent heat is commonly measured in **Joules (J)**, and its value depends on the substance's physical properties and phase transition.
 
• **Example Values:** The latent heat of fusion for ice is **334,000 J/kg**, while the latent heat of vaporization for water is approximately **2,260,000 J/kg**.
 
• **Scientific Significance:** Understanding latent heat is fundamental to thermodynamics, phase equilibria, and material science.
 
• **Practical Use:** This concept is utilized in designing systems like **heat exchangers**, **thermal storage devices**, and **cryogenic cooling systems**.

questions.question: The India met with an economic crisis in 1991 relating to ____.

options.text: shortfall in agriculture output due to severe drought

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**its external debt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **India's Economic Crisis of 1991:** The crisis stemmed primarily from an unsustainable level of **external debt**. By mid-1991, India’s **foreign exchange reserves** had plummeted to nearly $1 billion, which was insufficient to finance imports for even two weeks.
 
• The external debt had accumulated due to **excessive borrowing from foreign lenders**, leading to repayment obligations that India could not meet without further borrowing or drastic measures.
 
• The situation worsened with the **Gulf War (1990-91)**, which caused a spike in oil prices and disrupted foreign exchange inflows, further exacerbating the crisis.
 
• India was forced to pledge **67 tons of gold** to the Bank of England and other lenders to secure emergency loans to stabilize its economy.
 
• This crisis led to significant economic reforms, including the introduction of the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) policies**, aimed at restructuring the economy and reducing dependence on external debt.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Details on External Debt:**

 
 
• External debt refers to the total borrowing a country owes to foreign creditors, including governments, financial institutions, and private lenders.
 
• During the crisis, India's debt-servicing obligations (interest and principal repayments) exceeded its ability to pay, leading to a **balance of payments (BoP) problem**.
 
• The external debt burden was further aggravated by a **trade deficit**, where imports exceeded exports, draining foreign exchange reserves.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms Post-1991:**
 
 
• The crisis prompted India to adopt far-reaching economic reforms under Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• Key reforms included reducing trade barriers, deregulating industries, privatizing state-owned enterprises, and liberalizing foreign investment policies.
 
• These reforms marked a shift from a socialist economy to a more market-oriented economy.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Gulf War:**
 
 
• The **1990-91 Gulf War** disrupted oil supplies, causing oil prices to surge and straining India's import bill.
 
• Reduced remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf further impacted foreign exchange inflows.
 
 
 
• **Role of IMF and World Bank:**
 
 
• India approached the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** for a bailout package, which came with conditions for economic reforms.
 
• The IMF provided $2.2 billion in loans, while the World Bank also extended support for structural adjustments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**

 
 
• **Internal debt:** While internal debt was present, it did not directly trigger the 1991 crisis.
 
• **Trade embargo:** No trade embargo from Western countries existed during this period.
 
• **Shortfall in agricultural output:** Agriculture faced challenges, but these were not the primary cause of the crisis.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:** The 1991 crisis is considered a turning point in India's economic history, leading to the modernization of its economy.
 
• **Key Figures:** The reforms were spearheaded by **Dr. Manmohan Singh**, who is regarded as the architect of India's economic liberalization.

questions.question: In which of the following years Mahatma Gandhi led the Champaran Movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1917**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Champaran Movement**, led by **Mahatma Gandhi**, began in the year **1917**.
 
• The movement was initiated to address the grievances of the **indigo farmers** of the Champaran district in Bihar.
 
• Under the **tinkathia system**, farmers were forced to grow indigo on a portion of their land (three out of twenty parts) and sell it at prices fixed by the British planters, which caused severe economic exploitation.
 
• Mahatma Gandhi, after being persuaded by local leaders like **Rajkumar Shukla**, visited Champaran to investigate the plight of the farmers.
 
• The movement led to the **abolition of the tinkathia system** and marked Gandhi’s first significant political victory in India, establishing him as a major leader in the Indian freedom struggle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Significance of Champaran Movement:**

 
 
• The Champaran Movement is considered the **first Satyagraha** led by Mahatma Gandhi in India.
 
• It was a non-violent campaign that focused on truth and moral force to achieve justice for the oppressed farmers.
 
• It demonstrated the effectiveness of mass civil disobedience and became a template for future struggles in India’s freedom movement.
 
 
 
• **Tinkathia System:**
 
 
• Under this system, farmers were compelled to grow indigo on a part of their land, which was used for dye production.
 
• The system caused economic hardships as farmers were paid meager amounts and could not grow food crops on the land forced for indigo cultivation.
 
 
 
• **Role of Local Leaders:**
 
 
• **Rajkumar Shukla**, a local farmer from Champaran, played a significant role in bringing Gandhi to the region to address the plight of farmers.
 
• Other key figures like **Rajendra Prasad**, who later became the first President of India, and **Anugrah Narayan Sinha**, also supported the movement.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Movement:**
 
 
• The success of the Champaran Satyagraha inspired confidence in the Indian masses about their ability to challenge British authority.
 
• It marked the beginning of Gandhi’s leadership in the Indian freedom movement and established the principle of non-violent resistance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Background to the Movement:**

 
 
• Indigo cultivation was introduced by the British in India during the colonial period.
 
• The demand for indigo declined after the invention of synthetic dyes in Germany, but British planters continued to exploit Indian farmers.
 
 
 
• **Gandhi’s Methodology:**
 
 
• Gandhi adopted the method of **fact-finding and negotiation** with the British authorities to resolve the issues.
 
• He also encouraged farmers to speak up about their grievances, empowering them politically and socially.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• The Champaran Movement set the stage for subsequent struggles such as the Kheda Satyagraha (1918) and the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
 
• It also marked the beginning of Gandhi’s rise as a prominent leader in India’s fight for independence.

questions.question: Which of the following five year plan of India started in 1969?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fourth Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Fourth Five-Year Plan** of India was implemented from **1969 to 1974**. It was the first plan after the **Green Revolution**, focusing on agricultural productivity and self-sufficiency.
 
• The plan aimed at achieving **economic stability** and emphasizing the removal of poverty through self-reliance and increased production.
 
• During this period, India faced challenges such as a **food crisis** and **inflation**, which influenced the plan's objectives and strategies.
 
• The policy measures in the Fourth Plan were also shaped by external events such as the **Bangladesh Liberation War**, which required significant economic and defense resources.
 
• This plan marked the beginning of efforts to strengthen **industrialization**, alongside the continuation of emphasis on agriculture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **First Five-Year Plan:**

 
 
• Implemented during **1951-1956**, it focused on **agriculture**, irrigation, and energy infrastructure as the primary areas of development.
 
• The plan was based on the **Harrod-Domar model** and aimed to address the food shortage and post-independence economic challenges.
 
• Key achievements included the establishment of dams such as **Bhakra Nangal** and the initiation of community development programs.
 
 
 
• **Second Five-Year Plan:**
 
 
• Implemented during **1956-1961**, it focused on rapid industrialization and the development of the **public sector**.
 
• The plan followed the **Mahalanobis model**, emphasizing heavy industries and capital goods production.
 
• Key initiatives included the establishment of steel plants in **Bhilai, Rourkela, and Durgapur**.
 
 
 
• **Fourth Five-Year Plan:**
 
 
• Focused on achieving **self-reliance** and alleviating poverty through agriculture and industrial development.
 
• Introduced measures to control **inflation** and stabilize the economy amidst global economic challenges.
 
• Marked by significant events like the **Bangladesh Liberation War** and the oil crisis.
 
 
 
• **Sixth Five-Year Plan:**
 
 
• Implemented during **1980-1985**, emphasizing economic liberalization and poverty alleviation.
 
• Focused on technological upgradation, infrastructure development, and expanding employment opportunities.
 
• Introduced new initiatives like the **Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Green Revolution:** The Fourth Five-Year Plan was influenced by the **Green Revolution**, which significantly increased agricultural productivity in India, particularly in wheat production.
 
• **Bangladesh Liberation War:** India’s involvement in the **1971 Bangladesh Liberation War** led to financial constraints, impacting the implementation of certain development programs during the plan.
 
• **Inflation Control:** The plan included measures to combat **high inflation rates**, which were a result of the rising costs of imports and defense spending.
 
• **Focus on Self-Reliance:** The emphasis on **self-reliance** in agriculture and industries aimed to reduce dependency on foreign imports and establish a robust domestic economy.
 
• **Social Equity:** Programs to address poverty and improve the living conditions of the population were integral to the plan’s objectives.

questions.question:
Which of the following was the key issue during launch of eighth five year plan of India?

I. Worsening balance of payment position.

II. Rising debt burden.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Eighth Five Year Plan** (1992-1997) was delayed due to the economic crisis India faced in 1991. This period saw the implementation of economic reforms and liberalization policies.
 
• The **worsening balance of payment position** was a major challenge. India faced a severe **foreign exchange crisis** in 1991, with foreign exchange reserves dwindling to cover only two weeks of imports. *Hence, statement I is correct.*
 
• The country was burdened with a **rising debt**, leading to difficulty in meeting repayment obligations. The external debt had surged, and debt servicing consumed a significant portion of the GDP. *Hence, statement II is correct.*
 
• The government adopted structural reforms to resolve these issues, focusing on **economic liberalization**, reducing fiscal deficits, and attracting foreign investment.
 
• Both factors—**balance of payment crisis** and **rising debt burden**—were key issues that defined the strategies and priorities of the Eighth Five Year Plan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Balance of Payment Crisis (1991):**

 
 
• India faced a severe **economic crisis** in 1991 due to high fiscal deficits, excessive borrowing, and a trade imbalance.
 
• The **current account deficit** widened, leading to the depletion of foreign exchange reserves to dangerously low levels.
 
• To address the crisis, India sought assistance from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and implemented structural adjustment programs.
 
 
 
• **Rising Debt Burden:**
 
 
• India's **external debt** increased significantly during the late 1980s and early 1990s, causing strain on the economy.
 
• The **debt service ratio** (the proportion of export earnings used to repay debt) rose to unsustainable levels.
 
• Efforts were made to reduce fiscal deficits and enhance export performance to manage the debt burden.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms of 1991:**
 
 
• The crisis led to the introduction of **New Economic Policy** in 1991, focusing on **liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG)**.
 
• These reforms were aimed at improving the balance of payments, reducing fiscal deficits, and fostering economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Eighth Five Year Plan (1992-1997):**
 
 
• The plan emphasized **human resource development, poverty alleviation**, and **self-reliance**.
 
• Key focus areas included **agriculture, industry, and infrastructure development**.
 
• The plan also prioritized **export promotion** and **foreign direct investment** to address the balance of payment issues.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Strategies Adopted:**

 
 
• India adopted **structural reforms** to stabilize the economy, including reducing subsidies and enhancing tax revenue.
 
• Focus was placed on **export-oriented industries** to boost foreign exchange earnings.
 
 
 
• **IMF Assistance:**
 
 
• India pledged **gold reserves** to secure a loan from the IMF to manage its foreign exchange crisis.
 
• The conditions attached to the loan required India to undertake significant economic reforms.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Reforms:**
 
 
• The reforms led to a gradual improvement in India's economic indicators, including **growth in GDP** and **foreign exchange reserves**.
 
• However, challenges such as inflation and social inequality persisted.

questions.question: The first export processing zone in India was set up in which of the following year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1965**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

 
• The first **Export Processing Zone (EPZ)** in India was established in **Kandla, Gujarat** in the year **1965**. This marked the beginning of India's efforts to boost exports and attract foreign investments.
 
• The primary objective of setting up EPZs was to promote **export-oriented industrialization** and generate employment opportunities in the country.
 
• Kandla EPZ was designed to provide an integrated infrastructure for industries with facilities such as warehouses, export-import services, and customs clearance, simplifying the process for exporters.
 
• EPZs were the precursor to the modern **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)**, which were introduced later in the 2000s to further enhance India's export competitiveness.
 
• Globally, EPZs have been utilized as a strategy to attract **foreign direct investment (FDI)** and boost exports, and India adopted this model to integrate into the global trade system.

questions.question: In India's gender budget,———— provision. includes schemes where the budgetary allocation for women and girls is below 30% of the total
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Part C**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gender Budgeting in India**: The Government of India introduced gender budgeting as a tool to assess and address the gender-based needs in public expenditure.
 
• Gender Budget is divided into two parts: **Part A** includes schemes with 100% allocation for women, and **Part C** includes schemes where **budget allocation for women and girls is below 30%** of the total scheme budget.
 
• **Part C Schemes**: These are significant as they address the needs of women in broader development schemes where their representation is below 30% of total allocation.
 
• The categorization helps policymakers focus on **both direct and indirect benefits** for women and girls in various schemes and initiatives.
 
• Examples of schemes under **Part C** include programs in sectors like agriculture, education, health, and rural development where women are beneficiaries but the allocation does not exceed 30%.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **What is Gender Budgeting?**:

 
 
• Gender budgeting is a **gender-based assessment** of budgets, ensuring that public resources are allocated in a way that benefits women and men equally.
 
• It was introduced in India in **2005-06** to promote gender equity in development.
 
 
 
• **Structure of India's Gender Budget:**
 
 
• **Part A:** Includes schemes where 100% of the allocation benefits women. Examples include schemes for women’s health, empowerment, and education.
 
• **Part B:** Covers schemes where at least **30% to 99% of the allocation** benefits women.
 
• **Part C:** Includes schemes where allocation for women and girls is below **30%** of the total allocation.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Gender Budgeting:**
 
 
• Ensures equitable distribution of public funds.
 
• Promotes **women's empowerment** and their active participation in economic development.
 
• Addresses gaps in access to resources and opportunities for women.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Gender Budget Initiatives:**
 
 
• **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao Scheme**: Focuses on improving the status of the girl child.
 
• **National Rural Health Mission**: Includes maternal health programs.
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)**: Provides employment opportunities with a focus on women workers.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **India's Gender Budgeting History:** India introduced gender budgeting in **2005-06** as part of its commitment to achieving **gender equality** and promoting women’s empowerment.
 
• **Global Perspective:** Gender budgeting is adopted worldwide, including countries like **Australia, South Africa, and Sweden**, to address gender disparities in public spending.
 
• **Challenges in Implementation:** Despite progress, challenges include **lack of awareness**, insufficient data, and inadequate monitoring mechanisms.
 
• **Policy Recommendations:** To strengthen gender budgeting, policymakers emphasize **capacity building**, better data collection, and integrating gender concerns into mainstream planning processes.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement is correct regarding the plant hormones?

I. They help to coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment.

II. They are synthesised at places away from where they act and simply diffuse to the area of action
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plant hormones:** Plant hormones, also known as phytohormones, are chemical substances that significantly influence various physiological processes in plants, such as growth, development, and environmental responses.
 
• **Statement I:** "They help to coordinate growth, development, and responses to the environment" is **correct**. Plant hormones regulate processes like cell elongation, flowering, fruit ripening, and stress responses, ensuring plants adapt to changing environmental conditions.
 
• **Statement II:** "They are synthesized at places away from where they act and simply diffuse to the area of action" is **incorrect**. While some plant hormones like auxins are produced in specific regions (e.g., shoot tips) and transported to the target site, not all hormones follow this mechanism. Cytokinins, for example, are synthesized in roots and transported upward via xylem. The movement of hormones often involves active transport rather than simple diffusion.
 
• **Examples:** Auxins promote cell elongation, gibberellins regulate stem elongation, and ethylene controls fruit ripening. These demonstrate how plant hormones coordinate growth and environmental adaptations.
 
• **Correct Option:** Based on the explanation, only Statement I is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Plant Hormones:**

 
 
• **Auxins:** Promote cell elongation, apical dominance, and root initiation. Example: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA).
 
• **Gibberellins:** Stimulate stem elongation, seed germination, and flowering. Example: GA3.
 
• **Cytokinins:** Promote cell division and delay leaf senescence. Example: Zeatin.
 
• **Ethylene:** A gaseous hormone responsible for fruit ripening, flower wilting, and leaf abscission.
 
• **Abscisic Acid (ABA):** Induces dormancy and regulates stress responses like drought tolerance.
 
 
 
• **Plant Hormone Transport:**
 
 
• Hormones like auxins move via polar transport, whereas cytokinins are transported through vascular tissues.
 
• Active transport mechanisms involve specific proteins, ensuring hormones reach target sites effectively.
 
 
 
• **Key Functions:**
 
 
• **Growth regulation:** Hormones control cell division, elongation, and differentiation.
 
• **Environmental adaptation:** Hormones help plants respond to stress, light, and gravity.
 
• **Developmental processes:** They regulate flowering, fruiting, seed germination, and dormancy.
 
 
 
• **Examples in Agriculture:**
 
 
• **Auxins:** Used in rooting powders and herbicides.
 
• **Ethylene:** Utilized for artificial fruit ripening.
 
• **Gibberellins:** Applied to increase fruit size in crops like grapes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Discovery:** Auxins were first discovered by Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin in their experiments on phototropism in canary grass.
 
• **Significance in Crop Improvement:** Genetic engineering of hormone pathways is used to enhance crop yield and stress tolerance.
 
• **Stress Hormones:** Abscisic Acid (ABA) is crucial for drought resistance, helping plants conserve water during adverse conditions.
 
• **Global Applications:** Plant hormones are integral to modern agricultural practices, including tissue culture and hybrid seed production.

questions.question: The term "Jambudvipa" used in Mahabharata is associated with which tree?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Banyan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The term **"Jambudvipa"** is extensively mentioned in ancient Indian texts, including the **Mahabharata**, and is associated with the Indian subcontinent. The name "Jambudvipa" translates to the "Island of the Jambu Tree."
 
• The **Jambu tree** mentioned in ancient texts is identified as the **Banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis)**, which holds significant cultural and spiritual value in India.
 
• The Banyan tree is considered sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, symbolizing **immortality, wisdom, and shelter**. It is often refe
